#10644. CORS Error Fix: Diagnose Console Errors and Configure Headers

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Every frontend developer will eventually stare at a CORS error in the browser console, watching an API call fail for reasons that seem opaque. A CORS error fix requires understanding what the browser is actually telling you, matching that specific message to its root cause, and applying a targeted, security-conscious server configuration.

The scheme, host, and port together define an "origin." https://example.com and http://example.com are different origins (different schemes), as are https://example.com and https://api.example.com (different hosts). https://example.com and https://example.com:443 are the same origin because port 443 is the default for HTTPS, and browsers omit it in origin comparisons. The browser enforces the same-origin policy on client-side JavaScript reading responses, not on sending requests. This distinction trips up many developers: the server may still receive and fully process the request; the browser simply refuses to expose the response to the calling code. The request lands, the database row gets written, and the browser throws an error anyway. The policy exists to prevent a malicious page from silently reading sensitive data from another origin using the user's ambient credentials.

Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) is a controlled opt-in mechanism via HTTP response headers. The server signals to the browser that a specific foreign origin is permitted to read its responses. Four headers control the mechanism: Access-Control-Allow-Origin specifies which origin is allowed, and Access-Control-Allow-Methods declares which HTTP methods are permitted. Access-Control-Allow-Headers lists which custom or non-simple headers the client may send, while Access-Control-Allow-Credentials indicates whether the browser should expose the response to credentialed requests.

The browser does not treat all cross-origin requests equally. "Simple" requests use GET, HEAD, or POST with a Content-Type of application/x-www-form-urlencoded, multipart/form-data, or text/plain, and no custom headers. A POST with Content-Type: application/json is not a simple request and triggers a preflight.

Simple requests go directly to the server, and the browser evaluates the CORS headers on the response. Anything else triggers a preflight request: an OPTIONS call the browser sends automatically before the actual request, asking the server whether the real request would be acceptable. If the OPTIONS response lacks the proper CORS headers, the browser never sends the real request at all.

A typical Chrome DevTools error reads: Access to fetch at 'https://api.example.com/data' from origin 'https://app.example.com' has been blocked by CORS policy: No 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header is present on the requested resource.

Two origins appear in this message. The URL after "fetch at" is the target server, the resource the code tried to reach. The value after "from origin" is the page's own origin, the one making the request. Chrome is stating that the target server's response did not include an Access-Control-Allow-Origin header that matches the requesting origin, so the browser blocked the response from reaching JavaScript.

The most common variant is the missing header: No 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header is present on the requested resource. The server simply did not include the header at all.

When the console says Response to preflight request doesn't pass access control check, the server either did not respond to the OPTIONS request correctly or returned a non-2xx status code for it.

Redirect variant: Redirect is not allowed for a preflight request. Developers commonly misdiagnose this one. It occurs when the URL triggers a redirect before reaching the application handler. Typical culprits include HTTP-to-HTTPS upgrades, trailing-slash normalization (e.g., /api/data redirecting to /api/data/), or a load balancer rewriting URLs. The browser's preflight OPTIONS request follows the redirect, and the Fetch specification (§4.8) forbids following redirects on preflight requests, so the entire flow fails. Fix the URL so no redirect occurs.

Credential variant: The value of the 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header must not be the wildcard '*' when the request's credentials mode is 'include'. When fetch is called with credentials: 'include' or XMLHttpRequest sets withCredentials = true, the server must respond with the exact requesting origin, not *. The browser will block JavaScript access to the response if a wildcard is used with credentials.

Entry point: What does the console error say?

Each branch leads to a specific fix section in this article. Bookmark this decision tree and start here every time a CORS error surfaces.

Before modifying any server code, verify what the server actually returns by simulating a preflight request from the command line:

The -i flag prints response headers. -X OPTIONS sets the HTTP method to OPTIONS, mimicking the browser's preflight. The Origin header declares the requesting origin. Access-Control-Request-Method tells the server which method the real request would use. Access-Control-Request-Headers lists the custom headers the real request would include.

If these are absent, the server is not configured for CORS. If the response is a 301 or 302 redirect, the redirect variant is the culprit.

During local development, the least-configuration way to eliminate cross-origin issues is to proxy API requests through the dev server so the browser sees all traffic as same-origin.

With this configuration, a fetch('/api/users') call from the frontend at http://localhost:5173 is forwarded to http://localhost:3001/users. The browser never sees a cross-origin request. Without changeOrigin: true, the Host header sent upstream retains the dev server's hostname, which may cause backend rejections if the target validates the Host header. This is strictly a development-only solution. Production builds served from a static host will not have this proxy, so proper server-side CORS headers remain necessary.

Tested with: cors@2.8.5, express@4.18, Node.js 20 LTS. The cors package API surface has been stable since 2.x; check the changelog if you are on an earlier major version.

The simplest fix to unblock development uses the cors npm package with its defaults:

This applies Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * to every response. It unblocks any requesting origin, but it cannot be used with credentialed requests, and it exposes every endpoint to every origin on the internet. Any page an attacker controls can issue authenticated requests to your API and read the responses if the user is logged in. Move past it quickly.

For production, validate the incoming Origin header against an allowlist and reflect only permitted origins:

The origin function receives the Origin header value and calls callback(null, true) to allow the request. When true is passed, the cors package automatically reflects the incoming Origin header in the Access-Control-Allow-Origin response header and sets Vary: Origin. This satisfies the credential requirement and prevents open CORS misconfiguration. Setting credentials: true in the options causes the middleware to include the Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true response header. The cors middleware automatically handles OPTIONS preflight responses when applied at the app level.

Tested with: Next.js 14.x App Router, Node.js 20 LTS. The OPTIONS handler behavior and middleware matcher syntax changed between Next.js 13 and 15; exporting an explicit OPTIONS handler is the safest cross-version approach.

The cors npm package does not plug directly into the Next.js App Router (as of Next.js 13+). Instead, set headers manually in a route handler:

The OPTIONS export explicitly handles preflight requests and returns a 204 No Content with the required CORS headers. Without this, Next.js returns a 405 Method Not Allowed for OPTIONS in some versions (the exact behavior changed between 13 and 14), triggering the preflight failure variant. Exporting an explicit OPTIONS handler is the safest cross-version approach. The getCorsHeaders function returns an empty object for disallowed or absent origins, ensuring that server capabilities (supported methods and headers) are not disclosed to untrusted origins.

For projects with many API routes, centralizing CORS logic in middleware avoids repetition:

The matcher restricts this middleware to API routes only. Access-Control-Max-Age instructs browsers to cache preflight results. Chrome caps this value at 7200 seconds (2 hours); Firefox honors up to 86400. The Vary: Origin header is only set when a cross-origin request is detected (the Origin header is present and allowed), avoiding unnecessary CDN cache fragmentation on same-origin or server-to-server requests. CORS headers including Access-Control-Allow-Methods and Access-Control-Allow-Headers are only sent to allowed origins, preventing server capability disclosure to untrusted origins.

Tested with: Nginx 1.24+. The map directive behavior is stable across modern Nginx versions.

When Nginx sits in front of a backend, it is often the right place to manage CORS centrally. Important: Do not use if with add_header inside a location block -- Nginx's if block causes all parent-scope add_header directives to be silently ignored, breaking CORS headers on actual (non-OPTIONS) API responses.

The map directive builds an allowlist: if $http_origin matches a listed value, $cors_origin is set to that value; otherwise it remains empty. The always parameter ensures headers are added even on error responses (4xx, 5xx), which is critical because Nginx's add_header without always silently drops headers on non-2xx responses.

Nginx's if directive creates a new configuration context. Any add_header inside an if block discards all add_header directives from the enclosing scope.

Why the if block contains all headers and return 204: By placing return 204 inside the if block, the OPTIONS request is fully handled there and never reaches the outer add_header directives or proxy_pass. Non-OPTIONS requests skip the if block entirely and the outer scope's add_header directives and proxy_pass handle them. This separation avoids the inheritance pitfall: each request path (OPTIONS vs. non-OPTIONS) has its own complete, self-contained set of headers.

Note on empty $cors_origin: When the allowlist excludes the origin, $cors_origin resolves to an empty string, and Nginx emits Access-Control-Allow-Origin: (a blank header). Browsers will reject CORS for the request, which is the correct security outcome. However, emitting a blank header is technically non-conformant with RFC 6454. The most robust production solution is to handle CORS in the application layer (Express/Next.js) and have Nginx proxy transparently, or to use OpenResty/Lua for conditional header suppression.

After deploying, verify that both curl -X OPTIONS and curl -X GET against the same URL return the expected CORS headers.

A frequent source of the redirect CORS variant is a proxy_pass trailing-slash mismatch. If the location block is location /api but proxy_pass is http://127.0.0.1:3001 (no trailing slash), Nginx may issue a redirect for /api/ normalization before the request reaches the handler. Similarly, a return 301 https://... rule placed before the CORS location block can redirect the OPTIONS preflight. The fix is straightforward: ensure trailing slashes match between location and proxy_pass, and place any redirect rules after or outside the API location block so they do not intercept OPTIONS requests.

Use an explicit origin allowlist. Avoid * when credentials are involved; the browser will block JavaScript access to the response if a wildcard is used with credentials: 'include'.

Restrict Access-Control-Allow-Methods to only the methods the API actually uses. Listing every HTTP method widens the attack surface unnecessarily.

Set Access-Control-Max-Age to cache preflight responses. Chrome caps this value at 7200 seconds (2 hours); Firefox honors up to 86400 (24 hours). Use 7200 as a safe cross-browser default, or 86400 if your users are primarily on Firefox and you want fewer preflight round-trips.

Include Vary: Origin on every response where Access-Control-Allow-Origin is set conditionally. Without it, CDN or proxy caches may serve a CORS response cached for one origin to a different origin, causing intermittent failures.

Never mirror the request Origin header back without validating it against an allowlist. This is an open CORS misconfiguration that effectively disables the same-origin policy for any attacker-controlled origin.

Do not install browser extensions that disable CORS either -- they mask the problem during development and expose you to real cross-origin attacks on every other site you visit.

Avoid adding CORS headers in both the application framework and Nginx simultaneously. Duplicate Access-Control-Allow-Origin headers cause the browser's CORS origin comparison to fail; the browser receives the response but blocks JavaScript from reading it, producing the same CORS error the fix was meant to resolve.

Read the console error, match it against the decision tree, apply the targeted fix, and verify with the curl preflight command. Use the decision tree above as a reference for every future CORS error.

#10639. Building Accessible Navigation Menus with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Navigation is one of the most important components of a website. It helps visitors discover content, move between pages, and understand how a site is organized. However, a navigation menu that works well with a mouse may create problems for keyboard users, people who rely on screen readers, or visitors using small mobile screens.

Building an accessible navigation menu involves more than adding a few ARIA attributes or increasing the size of clickable elements. Developers need to consider semantic HTML, keyboard interaction, visible focus indicators, responsive layouts, and predictable behavior.

In this tutorial, we will build a responsive navigation menu using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. We will also examine common accessibility mistakes and explain how to test the finished component.

HTML provides several native elements that communicate the purpose and structure of a navigation interface.

A website's primary navigation should generally use a

element containing a list of links. This structure helps browsers and assistive technologies identify the navigation region and understand the available destinations.

The aria-label gives the navigation landmark a descriptive name. This becomes particularly useful when a page contains multiple navigation regions, such as a primary menu and a footer menu.

Using a list also communicates that the links form a related group. Each link has a meaningful destination, making it possible for visitors to navigate the site without relying on visual positioning alone.

A common mistake is using clickable

elements instead of links. Although JavaScript can make a div respond to clicks, it does not automatically provide the same keyboard behavior and navigation semantics as an anchor element.

For navigation to another page, use an anchor. For an action that changes the interface, use a button.

A navigation menu should adapt to the available screen width without hiding important links or creating horizontal scrolling.

The following CSS creates a flexible desktop navigation layout:

Flexbox aligns the logo and navigation horizontally while allowing the link list to wrap when necessary.

The gap property controls the spacing between links without requiring individual margins. Removing the list markers also produces a cleaner navigation layout while preserving the underlying list semantics.

Notice that the hover style includes an underline as well as a color change. This provides an additional visual cue instead of relying exclusively on color.

However, hover effects alone are insufficient because touchscreens do not have conventional hover behavior, and keyboard users do not navigate with a mouse.

Many visitors use the Tab key to move between interactive elements. A navigation menu should make the currently focused link easy to identify.

The :focus-visible pseudo-class allows browsers to display a focus indicator when it is appropriate, particularly during keyboard navigation.

Avoid removing the browser's default outline unless you replace it with a clearly visible alternative.

Keyboard accessibility also depends on the HTML structure. Standard anchor elements already support keyboard focus and activation, so the basic navigation above does not need custom JavaScript keyboard handlers.

That is an important design principle: use native browser behavior wherever possible rather than recreating it unnecessarily.

On smaller screens, a horizontal navigation menu may occupy too much space. A toggle button can provide a compact alternative while preserving access to the links.

The menu button is hidden on larger screens and displayed on smaller ones. On mobile, the navigation links are initially hidden until JavaScript adds the is-open class.

The aria-expanded attribute communicates whether the menu is currently expanded, while aria-controls identifies the element controlled by the button.

These attributes must reflect the actual interface state. Adding them without updating their values when the menu opens and closes can confuse assistive technology users.

The JavaScript should update both the visual state and the accessibility information when the user activates the button.

When the button is clicked, the code reads the current state, reverses it, updates aria-expanded, and toggles the CSS class.

Because the button is a native HTML button, it already supports keyboard activation. There is no need to add separate Enter or Space key handlers.

For a production implementation, you should also consider what happens when the viewport changes from mobile to desktop. For example, if the menu is open on mobile and the visitor resizes the browser, the desktop layout should not remain in an inconsistent state.

A more complete implementation can synchronize the menu state with the responsive breakpoint, close the menu when a navigation link is selected, and ensure that hidden links cannot be reached through keyboard navigation.

A navigation menu may look correct and still be difficult to use. Testing should cover both automated checks and real interactions.

Start with keyboard testing. Use Tab and Shift+Tab to move through the logo, menu button, and navigation links. Check that focus indicators are visible and that the order follows the visual and logical structure.

The menu button appears at the intended breakpoint.

Activating the button opens and closes the navigation.

The aria-expanded value matches the visible state.

Hidden links are not available for keyboard interaction while the menu is closed.

Selecting a link takes the visitor to the correct destination.

You can also use accessibility inspection tools to identify missing accessible names, invalid ARIA attributes, and other common problems.

Automated tools are useful, but they cannot establish that every interaction is understandable. Manual testing with a keyboard and, where possible, a screen reader remains important.

For larger websites, reusable navigation components and automated browser tests can help prevent accessibility regressions when styles or interaction logic change.

Accessible navigation starts with semantic HTML and builds on that foundation through responsive CSS, visible focus indicators, and carefully implemented JavaScript.

Native links and buttons provide much of the expected keyboard behavior automatically. Responsive styles make the menu usable across screen sizes, while accurate ARIA state helps communicate whether a collapsible menu is open or closed.

The most reliable approach is to keep the implementation as simple as possible, use browser features instead of recreating them, and test the actual experience rather than relying only on how the interface looks.

When accessibility is considered from the beginning, navigation becomes easier to maintain and more usable for a wider range of visitors.

#10633. What “Clear Form” Should Really Do: Managing Draft Data in JavaScript

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

A user fills out a form, requests a preview, and then changes their mind. They click “Clear,” the inputs become empty, and the interface appears ready for someone else.

A moment later, the previous preview returns.

The application cleared the fields, but an asynchronous request still held the old values and updated the screen when it finished. Similar problems occur when drafts remain in browser storage, validation messages retain personal details, or a component’s internal state survives a visual reset.

For developers building onboarding, expense, application, and document workflows, clearing a form is a state-management operation. It deserves the same attention as submission.

This article explains how to define that operation, prevent stale results, and inspect the outcome using practical browser and testing tools.

Start by listing the places where a draft exists. The visible inputs are only one location.

When reviewing a financial-data interface, a useful design exercise is to map which information belongs to the current draft and what should happen when the user starts again. The same exercise applies to expense submissions and customer onboarding; the implementation must be assessed separately from the visible interface.

Name actions according to their actual scope. “Clear this form” should not imply that previously submitted records have been deleted. If a draft has been saved remotely, distinguish clearing the current screen from deleting the saved draft.

For a broader introduction to form structure and validation, SitePoint’s guide to modern HTML forms provides useful background.

Autosave is convenient, but persisting the entire form after every keystroke is an architectural decision, not a harmless UI enhancement.

For a short workflow, keeping the draft in memory may be sufficient. For a longer workflow, decide which fields may be retained, how the user understands that behavior, and when the retained copy is removed.

Browser storage options have different lifetimes. According to MDN’s sessionStorage documentation, session storage is associated with a page session and survives reloads. It should not be treated as equivalent to an ordinary variable that disappears when the page reloads.

Nor does shorter retention make storage a security boundary. The OWASP HTML5 security guidance cautions against storing sensitive information in local storage because JavaScript running in the origin can access it.

This reduces unnecessary copies. It does not provide secure memory erasure or protect a page from every script that can access its data.

The native form.reset() method restores controls to their default values. It does not necessarily make every field empty.

For example, an input rendered with a default value can return to that value after a reset. The method also does not clear a separate preview element, invalidate a network response, or update every framework-managed state variable.

Use a small HTML form with empty defaults for the following example:

The clear control uses type="button" so the application can coordinate the complete operation.

In a React or Vue implementation, apply the same policy to the state that controls the inputs. Clearing the DOM while leaving the component state intact can cause the old values to reappear.

Cancellation helps reduce unnecessary work, but request identity is what protects the interface from a stale result.

Assign each request a generation number. Whenever the draft changes or is cleared, advance that number. A response may update the UI only if its number still matches the current generation.

The following JavaScript works with the HTML above. It assumes a same-origin POST /api/preview endpoint that accepts JSON and returns {"summary":"plain text"}. That endpoint is an integration requirement; it is not implemented here.

Editing a field also invalidates the preview. Otherwise, users could mistake a result based on earlier values for a result based on their current input.

The code writes server-provided text with textContent rather than interpreting it as HTML. It also displays a fixed failure message instead of echoing request values into an error.

AbortController allows the client to abort fetch-related work. Aborting a browser request does not guarantee that server processing stopped or that data already received by the server was deleted.

The generation check enforces the narrower promise: obsolete work must not update this interface. SitePoint’s introduction to the Fetch API explains the request and response mechanics behind the example.

The example intentionally does not save drafts. If your application does, add cleanup to the clear operation rather than assuming that resetting the form handles it.

Remove the application’s specific draft entry. Avoid localStorage.clear() as a general cleanup shortcut, since it also removes unrelated keys for that origin.

Keep the UI honest if storage cleanup fails. Do not announce that every saved copy is gone when the application has only emptied the visible controls.

An object URL should be revoked when it is no longer needed, but revoking it does not delete a file the user already downloaded.

For programmatic changes, call the same invalidation function used by input events. Assigning an input’s value in JavaScript does not automatically trigger the user-input event handler.

You do not need a large dependency stack to verify a clear operation. Each of these tools answers a different question.

Chrome’s local-storage inspection guide explains how to inspect stored entries. Check session storage and IndexedDB too if the application uses them; an empty local-storage table is not proof that no browser persistence exists.

Mock Service Worker is useful for creating reproducible response conditions during development. Use fictional fixtures so debugging sessions do not depend on real personal records.

With Playwright network interception, hold a preview response until the test explicitly releases it. Fill the form, request a preview, clear the draft, and only then release the response. Assert that the input remains empty and the preview never returns.

A controlled release is more reliable than hoping a fixed delay creates the right race. Also test two requests completing in reverse order.

A useful review checks the operation at several points:

Supplement automated accessibility checks with keyboard and screen-reader testing. The Playwright accessibility guide explains that automated checks detect only some accessibility problems.

Verify backend behavior separately. Server validation, authorization, retention, and deletion require their own implementation and tests. A clean browser interface cannot demonstrate those guarantees.

A reliable clear operation has a defined scope. It invalidates pending work, resets the application’s draft state, removes derived output, and handles persistence according to the product’s stated behavior.

The implementation can remain small. What matters is that the team knows where draft data lives and tests what happens when events arrive in an inconvenient order.

When developers make those boundaries explicit, “Clear form” becomes a predictable action rather than a visual reset that leaves the previous workflow running.

#10628. Best AI Brand Mention Tracking Tools for Enterprises in 2026: 6 Tools Compared

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

At a large company, the hard part of buying an AI brand mention tracking tool is procurement. IT asks about single sign-on, legal asks where the data sits, and the marketing team that wanted the tool waits weeks to log in. A pilot on one brand in one market looks cheap, then the other markets, the other teams and SSO arrive and the quote looks nothing like the trial.

That is why a generic "best tools" list helps enterprise buyers less than it should. All the tools below track how often ChatGPT, Gemini and Google's AI answers name your brand. What separates them at enterprise size is everything around the tracking: how many people can log in, how logins are controlled, whether the data can leave the tool and whether it copes with ten markets instead of one.

This guide compares six tools on those points. Peec AI ranks first because it combines unlimited users, enforceable SSO, source-level analysis and a published price ladder. The other five suit different buying situations.

AI brand mention tracking measures how often, where and how favourably AI engines name your brand when buyers ask category questions. A tool runs a fixed prompt set daily across engines such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Google AI Overviews, Google AI Mode and Microsoft Copilot, then reports mention rate (visibility), position inside the answer, sentiment, share of voice against competitors and the sources each answer cited.

For an enterprise, the answers differ by engine, country and product line, and a single visibility number hides most of that. Similarweb's May 2026 figures put ChatGPT at 53.9% of AI chatbot web visits, Gemini at 27.9% and Claude at 9.2%, against roughly 76% for ChatGPT in June 2025. The question "what does AI say about us?" is now spread over at least three engines.

Access and identity. Ask how many users each plan allows, whether SSO is available and on which plan, and whether you can enforce it. Most tools put SSO on their top tier or a custom plan, so budget for an enterprise contract early.

Markets and brands. Check whether the price grows per country, language or brand. Ten markets multiply a prompt set quickly.

Data access. The data has to reach the reporting leadership already reads: CSV export, an API, a BI connector or an MCP server.

Source analysis. A mention rate shows where you stand. Source data shows why, by listing the pages each engine read. Without it you cannot tell whether you are missing because nobody writes about you or because your own pages are not picked up.

Prompt volume and engines. A hundred to a hundred and fifty prompts per brand and market is a realistic start. Check which engines each plan includes and which sit behind add-ons.

Cost at your real workload. Price the tool for the users, markets and prompts you will have in a year, not for the pilot.

Enterprise teams rarely run on the entry tier, so the tables below price two realistic workloads: about 150 prompts, and about 350 prompts on ChatGPT, Google AI Overviews and Google AI Mode with 15 users, both tracked daily on three engines. Price per prompt is the monthly price divided by the prompts the plan includes. Rankscale and AthenaHQ price by answers or credits instead, so Rankscale's rows use the answer volume the workload needs: 150 prompts on three engines over 30 days is 13,500 answers a month, and 350 prompts is 31,500. Profound does not publish prices and is left out of the tables. Treat every figure as directional: enterprise contracts are custom and billed annually, so published self-serve prices show where a negotiation starts, not what you will pay.

Peec AI has the lowest price per prompt in the first table and the lowest monthly price in the second. Scrunch AI's Core plan costs $2.00 per prompt at 125 prompts and five users, and its larger plans are quote-only. Against Rankscale, the only other tool here with a published enterprise price, Peec AI costs 36% less at 150 prompts ($245 against $385) and 37% less at 350 prompts ($495 against $780). Rankscale does include more engines in its price, which Peec AI reserves for Enterprise. On ChatGPT plus both Google surfaces with 15 people logging in, Peec AI is the cheapest of the tools priced in these tables: $495 against $638 for Otterly.AI once Google AI Mode is added, and $780 for Rankscale. Otterly.AI and Rankscale include more engines in their price.

One thing changes these tables: single sign-on. Peec AI, Profound, AthenaHQ, Scrunch AI and Otterly.AI put SSO on Enterprise, and Rankscale puts it on a custom plan. If IT requires SSO, every tool here becomes a quote, and the published prices only show where the negotiation starts. Annual billing takes 15% to 17% off most of these.

Peec AI is a Berlin-based AI search analytics platform with a New York office. It tracks visibility, position, sentiment and share of voice, breaks every answer into the sources the engine read and turns the gaps it finds into prioritised actions. At enterprise scale its pricing is the main difference: users are unlimited on every plan, and Peec does not charge per country or language, with multi-country tracking from the Advanced plan.

Best for: Enterprise teams that want one tool for every market and every team, and need to know which pages to work on, not only where they stand.

Profound suits purchases that have to clear an information security review before anything else. It lists SOC 2, SSO and SAML on Enterprise, and it raised a $96M Series C at a $1B valuation in February 2026, which settles the vendor-risk question quickly.

Best for: Companies where compliance and vendor risk decide the purchase.

AthenaHQ was built by two former Google Search and DeepMind engineers. Its Enterprise plan has the longest feature list of the quote-based tools: SAML and OIDC single sign-on, audit logs, a 2-hour SLA, a dedicated Slack channel and executive dashboards that feed Tableau, Power BI and Looker. An optimisation agent drafts on-page and off-page actions, which suits large companies that have the analysis but not the hands to act on it.

Best for: Enterprises short on people to act on the data, who want BI dashboards and audit logs.

Scrunch AI publishes one self-serve plan and sells everything else through a quote. Core costs $250 a month and includes 125 prompts, 5,000 responses a month, five user licences and Google single sign-on, which is enough for a pilot with a small team.

Best for: Teams that want a published entry price and five users, with nine engines available on Enterprise.

Rankscale is the only tool here where the enterprise price is on the website. Enterprise is $780 a month for 12,000 credits, up to 48,000 answers, with REST API access and a dedicated partner. Claude, Copilot, ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, both Google surfaces, DeepSeek and Mistral are on every paid plan.

Best for: Teams that need a published enterprise price and the widest engine list.

Otterly.AI has the lowest entry price here, with unlimited team members on every plan and unlimited workspaces from the Standard plan, which helps when several business units want their own view. It is a lighter product than the five above, and SSO sits on its Enterprise plan, which starts from 1,000 prompts.

Best for: Business units that want their own workspace at a low price.

The most common mistake is buying for the pilot. A team runs a trial on one brand and one market, picks the tool with the friendliest entry price and finds out in month four that adding other markets, other teams and SSO moves them onto a quote that looks nothing like the trial.

Before you start a trial, write down three numbers: how many people will need to log in within a year, how many markets you sell in, and whether IT will require SSO. Then ask every vendor to price that.

Enterprise AI brand mention tracking is mostly a question of fit with how a large company buys. Peec AI is the strongest overall choice because users and markets do not drive its price, SSO can be enforced, and its source analysis shows what to fix instead of only how you rank.

Profound is the better route when a compliance review decides everything, AthenaHQ when you want BI dashboards and drafted work, Scrunch AI when you want a published entry price with five users, and Rankscale when you need a published enterprise price.

Whichever you pick, price your real workload, ask about SSO first and remember that the tool measures: what moves the number is being on the pages the engines read. The best AI brand mention tracking tools for enterprises are the ones that show you which pages those are.

What does an enterprise AI brand mention tracking tool cost?

Directionally, between $245 and $780 a month on published plans for 150 to 350 daily prompts: Peec AI Pro at $245 and Advanced at $495, Scrunch AI Core at $250 for 125 prompts, Otterly.AI Premium at $489 and Rankscale at $385 to $780. On Peec AI that is $1.41 to $1.63 per prompt with unlimited users. Once SSO is required, every tool here is a custom quote. The spread is driven by users and markets more than by features.

If more than a handful of people will log in, IT will usually ask for it. Every tool here puts SSO on Enterprise or a custom plan, so plan the budget for that contract instead of the self-serve tier.

How many prompts does an enterprise need?

A hundred to a hundred and fifty per brand and market. Start with the questions your sales team hears, then the comparisons buyers make between you and named competitors. More markets multiply the set. More product pages usually should not.

SEO usually owns the measurement. What breaks is the fix, because much of it means getting mentioned on sites you do not control, which sits with PR or communications. Agree that split before you buy.

LinkedIn doesn't publish a price for Recruiter or Recruiter Professional Services. Its Recruiter page says pricing "varies based on your organization's needs," and its plan comparison lists features, not prices. The figures below are reported by third-party pricing trackers and agencies that have seen quotes, so treat them as ranges and ask LinkedIn for a written quote. Pin's own LinkedIn Recruiter pricing breakdown covers each plan in more detail.

InMail and network details are from LinkedIn's plan comparison (October 2026). Prices are tracker-reported (July to September 2026), and annual Lite totals range from $1,680 to $2,040.

It depends on how much of your hiring runs through LinkedIn. One seat at the reported range costs about 1.8 to 2.4 times SHRM's 2025 benchmark of $5,475 average cost per hire for a nonexecutive role, so a seat has to contribute hires, not just searches. Teams weighing the lower-priced Lite plan can see where its limits start in Pin's guide to Recruiter Lite vs full Recruiter.

LinkedIn's January 2026 research found that two-thirds (66%) of recruiters say it has become harder to find qualified talent, and 93% plan to increase their use of AI in 2026.

A seat usually earns its cost when most of your candidates are on LinkedIn, you use the InMail allotment and your reply rates stay healthy.

LinkedIn is not standing still: Recruiter now builds search filters from a plain-language description, drafts AI-assisted messages and offers the Hiring Assistant add-on. The limits below are about design, checked against LinkedIn's pages in October 2026.

We checked each vendor's public pricing and product pages in October 2026. Pin is covered first because it spans the widest scope; the others follow in no ranked order.

Pin (pin.com) is an AI recruiting platform that handles candidate sourcing, outreach and interview scheduling in one product. For teams replacing LinkedIn Recruiter, Pin is the most direct one-tool replacement.

Best for: teams and agencies replacing LinkedIn Recruiter that want broader search, outreach and scheduling in one seat-priced tool with published prices. See also AI recruiting tools for agencies.

SeekOut is a sourcing platform for finding and engaging candidates across 1B+ profiles and your ATS. Its pricing page lists Sourcing Core at $179 a month, or $149 billed annually, with three seats, AI multi-step campaigns and a 14-day free trial; higher tiers are custom. The page lists email outreach and no interview scheduling.

Good for: small sourcing teams that want deep search, though outreach is email only, scheduling isn't listed and higher tiers are custom.

hireEZ is a talent acquisition platform that adds sourcing, CRM, outreach, screening and scheduling on top of your ATS. It lists 1B+ profiles across 45+ platforms, email, SMS and InMail engagement, and an AI Scheduler. Team pricing isn't published, and solo recruiters start at $494 a month.

Good for: mid-size and enterprise teams consolidating tools around an existing ATS, though team pricing is unpublished and solo starts at $494 a month.

Gem is a recruiting platform that layers a CRM, AI sourcing, outreach, scheduling and analytics on top of your ATS. It searches 800M+ profiles and runs multi-channel sequences, though its pricing page doesn't name the channels. Scheduling is an add-on to Gem + your ATS. Pricing is custom by headcount; the only published number is $130 a month for startups with 1 to 10 employees on yearly billing.

Good for: growth-stage and larger teams that want CRM and scheduling in one stack, though pricing is sales-led and scheduling is an add-on.

Findem is an AI talent-intelligence platform. Its site lists Multichannel Sourcing, a Talent CRM and a Scheduling Agent, and says it maps 1B+ career paths. Pricing isn't published; you request a demo.

Good for: larger talent teams that want attribute-rich search, though buying is demo-only and no price is published.

Fetcher is a sourcing platform that pairs a 500M+ candidate database with optional done-for-you sourcing. Its pricing page lists a custom Enterprise tier, Amplify at $649 a month on annual billing ($849 monthly), Growth at $379 ($499 monthly) and Self-serve at $115. It lists email outreach and a LinkedIn sourcing plugin, and no scheduling.

Good for: small teams that want extra sourcing capacity without building a process first, though scheduling isn't listed and the $115 entry tier jumps to $379.

"Not listed" means absent from the vendor's pricing page, not necessarily from the product.

If you are weighing a move, Pin's guide to leaving LinkedIn Recruiter covers how to run a side-by-side test.

Yes. Ryan Levy, Managing Partner at Cruit Group, says: "Pin gave us the ability to find candidates that didn't appear on LinkedIn Recruiter. The platform is easy to use and is continuing to evolve!" A common setup keeps one Recruiter seat for InMail and in-network reach, while Pin handles search across other sources, automated email sequences with LinkedIn and SMS tasks, the shared inbox and scheduling.

An illustration: five full Recruiter seats cost $50,000 to $65,000 a year at the reported range. One Recruiter seat plus five Pin Professional seats at $135 per month, billed annually, comes to $18,100 to $21,100, before InMail top-ups. Test on one open role first.

For tactics, see how to source passive candidates. For a wider list, see our earlier 12 best AI recruiting sourcing tools, whose April pricing predates these figures. Pin also publishes a Pin vs LinkedIn Recruiter comparison covering coverage, outreach and cost line by line.

Pin has a free plan with no credit card and paid plans from $99 a month, a fraction of a reported full Recruiter seat, and it also covers outreach and AI interview scheduling. hireEZ's solo plan starts at $494 a month, and SeekOut Sourcing Core is $149 a month billed annually with three seats.

LinkedIn doesn't publish list prices for Recruiter. Third-party pricing trackers put the full product at roughly $10,000 to $13,000 per seat per year, within a wider $9,000 to $15,000 range, and Recruiter Lite at about $170 a month. InMail top-ups and Hiring Assistant are extra, so ask for a written quote listing every line item.

It is worth it if most of your candidates are on LinkedIn, you use your InMail allotment and your response rates stay healthy. It is harder to justify for niche or technical talent active elsewhere, or when seats sit idle. Many teams keep one seat and add Pin for wider search, outreach and scheduling.

For multi-source reach, Pin's database is the broadest here: Pin says it searches 850M+ profiles from GitHub, Stack Overflow, patents and publications alongside professional networks and the broader web, with coverage across North America and Europe. SeekOut (1B+ profiles), hireEZ (1B+ across 45+ platforms) and Gem (800M+ profiles) also advertise multi-source databases. Of the tools here that also include multi-channel outreach and interview scheduling, Pin has the lowest published entry price: a free plan, then $99 a month.

Yes. Keep one LinkedIn Recruiter seat for InMail and in-network reach and let Pin handle the rest. Pin integrates with 120+ ATS platforms, so candidates from both tools can land in one pipeline.

LinkedIn Recruiter remains strong for in-network InMail, but its price is opaque and its reach stops at one network. Before renewing, audit seat usage, keep seats where InMail pays for itself and move search and outreach to a multi-source tool. For teams replacing LinkedIn Recruiter, Pin is the most direct one-tool replacement: multi-source search, automated email outreach with LinkedIn and SMS tasks, and scheduling at published prices. According to Pin's 2026 user survey, 91% of users reduced or eliminated LinkedIn Recruiter spend after switching to Pin.

#10615. AI Agents Need Idempotency: The Distributed Systems Problem Hiding Inside Agentic AI

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

A customer wants a $480 refund for a faulty part of a shipment he received. After waiting for 30 seconds for the payment API to process the refund, the customer support AI sends another request. It ultimately is fulfilled. However, as it turns out, the first request had also been fulfilled. The only thing missing was the notification of the refund for the customer. So the customer received two refunds of $480 each instead of the one he was asking for.

The AI was acting appropriately within its given constraints; the surrounding system couldn’t tell if the initial action had already been taken and failed to deliver the result. A well-known problem in distributed systems is gaining more notoriety as AI-powered agents increasingly perform actions beyond simply generating text. Idempotence is the solution to this problem.

Idempotence means an action can be performed multiple times with the same result as performing it once. This concept is particularly important for an AI agent that issues refunds, creates tickets, sends emails, or updates business applications.

AI agents as distributed software components have simple processes.

Think → choose a tool → call an API → receive a result → decide what to do next.

As we have outlined, many of the agent actions will utilize services and networks that can have issues from time to time. Consider the simple action of asking a payment provider to issue a refund. There are three possible outcomes:

The payment service never gets the request.

The refund went through, and the agent got the answer.

The refund went through, but the agent never received it back.

The most severe case, however, is when the time to complete an operation exceeds the timeout, but the operation does complete successfully. Since there is no answer, the software agent never learns of the operation's successful completion and must attempt to complete the operation again.

Distributed systems have dealt with the issues of unreliable networks for a long time already (retries, duplicate requests, etc.). By introducing agents, we give the software more freedom to choose when and how to proceed.

Consider an agent with these tools: search_customer(), check_inventory(), refund_payment(), send_email(), create_order(), delete_account()

Calling search_customer() twice will usually not cause much trouble.

In other words, an agent runtime should be able to tell if a tool only gets data or makes changes to the outside world. In the second group are things like sending money, getting money back, placing orders, writing messages, making accounts, and changing infrastructure.

There are side effects to these treatments. It's risky to think that agents can just retry every failed tool call as they get access to more business systems.

One common way to handle the duplicate requests issue is to implement idempotency keys.

Idempotency-Key: refund-order-123-run-842

The service stores the idempotency key and the result of processing the associated request.

It allows the refund to be processed the first time the idempotency key is sent to the service by the agent. Thereafter, if the response to the refund is lost and the agent attempts to resubmit the refund with the same idempotency key, the service will recognize that the refund has already been processed and return the previous result to the agent instead of processing another refund.

Many of the world’s leading payment companies, including Stripe, PayPal, and Square, use idempotency keys to allow their customers to safely retry requests.

However, one important rule for agents is that the agent software or workflow system—not the AI model—creates the idempotency key, and it is up to date.

By the time the model retries the same step, the Operation ID will have remained the same. This means the system can recognize the request as another attempt to execute the same action as before and not a new action.

Things could be easy if we could tell the model to ‘remember if it has already issued one of these before issuing another.' But even in the production environment, this approach is not sufficient. The agent could crash. The context could go away. The workflow could be taken off to be executed on another machine. The problem is that the model lacks sufficient information about what has or has not happened in external systems. Instead, the system should keep a record of the execution state outside of the model. The model determines what should happen. The runtime determines safe execution.

Modern agent tools include a name, description, and input parameters for the production system. More importantly, the agent runtime also needs to know about the behavior of the individual tool. For example, ‘refund_order’ modifies the application outside this tool, so the operation must be re-executed with the same actionID used for the initial failure. Also, as an example, refunds larger than $5,000 require manual approval. On the other hand, a ‘search_customer’ action is only a read, so re-execution can occur without human intervention. Based on this information, the OS makes decisions about the danger of the individual tool call. Automatic re-execution is still possible, even if the search fails. However, refunds require a bit more caution to avoid double posting of money. Thus, in addition to the input models for the AI tools used in real life, so-called “execution rules” are also required. These rules state when re-execution, increased security, or human intervention is required.

Suppose an AI agent were to perform the following three actions: 1) Make whole the customer, 2) Send a confirmation email with the order update and a proof, and 3) Check the status of the order in process. We had described how stopping the AI from paying out twice was only half the problem; the system also needed to know where the work had stopped. To that end, we’d like to introduce the concept of durable execution. For durable execution, the agent must do more than simply remember the actions it has taken. We need to keep track of the progress of the actions of the AI. The refund action was marked complete, but the email action was not sent yet. Thus, when the agent is restarted, it continues from where it left off rather than starting over. To create reliable AI agents, we need a few things: stable operation IDs, irrevocable actions, durable state, controlled retries, and logging. There are also cases where one wants to perform a recovery or compensating action (e.g., the agent makes a reservation but then fails to perform the subsequent action). The recovery action would be to cancel the reservation that had been made.

While controls with a person in the loop are mostly suitable for fine-grained actions that cannot be undone, idempotence ensures that an action is not accidentally executed more than once, and human approval is required to decide whether the action should be executed in the first place. This point is illustrated by an example: An employee correctly approves a $10,000 refund. However, the payment request somehow times out and is automatically re-executed several times. Without adequate idempotency security, the customer might end up with even more refunds than intended. Note, however, that a person’s approval cannot prevent double killing in such high-risk agent processes. Therefore, additional decision controls and corresponding execution controls are usually required to ensure that all actions are executed safely and correctly.

There are 5 simple questions that need to be answered before allowing an AI agent to take real-world actions.

Improving the model alone will not make the agent reliable unless we can answer all of these questions.

Much work in AI today focuses on making agents smarter, better at planning, and better to use as tools. But running agents in production has its own problems. API calls time out, processes crash, networks fail, and responses get lost, and the smartest agent can try again and again until it works. These are not new problems. Engineers working on distributed systems have been struggling with these same issues for decades. So long as the AI agent is confined to a simple test environment, of course it can query payment systems, customer information, and corporate tools. But when it is turned loose on the production corporation’s infrastructure (with all the payment systems, customer information, and corporate tools that entails), it must also be reliable. A smart model can figure out that a customer is due a refund. But a strong system can only give that customer a refund once. So the important question to ask of an AI agent before turning loose on it is, "Some powerful new tool: what happens if the action worked?" The answer will tell you whether or not the AI agent is currently able to operate reliably in production.

#10609. Web-Ready AI Images: Formats, Sizes, and srcset Done Right

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

AI image generation has become a normal part of many web projects. However, the image a model produces is rarely the image a browser should receive. A single large PNG straight from a generator can weigh several megabytes, ignore the visitor's screen size, and slow down your Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) before the page has a chance to impress anyone.

The good news is that the fix is not complicated. If you treat the generated image as a high-quality master file and run it through a small, repeatable pipeline, you can ship images that look sharp on every device and load quickly on slow connections.

This tutorial walks through that pipeline from start to finish: generating at the right size and aspect ratio, choosing modern formats, creating responsive variants with Node.js, writing srcset and sizes correctly, and avoiding the performance mistakes that show up most often in audits.

Image generators are built to produce visually impressive results, not optimized web assets. Their output is usually a single file at one resolution, often in PNG format, and sometimes with an aspect ratio that does not match your layout.

Sending that file directly to the browser creates three problems. First, mobile visitors download far more pixels than their screens can display. Second, PNG is a poor choice for photographic images because its lossless compression produces large files. Third, without width and height information, the browser cannot reserve space for the image, which causes layout shifts as the page loads.

A web pipeline solves all three. You generate one master image, export multiple sizes in modern formats, and let the browser choose the best version for each visitor.

Optimization starts before you export anything. The most efficient pipeline begins with an image that already fits your layout.

Look at where the image will appear and note its aspect ratio at each breakpoint. A full-width hero might use 16:9 on desktop, while a blog thumbnail might use 4:3 or 1:1. Then identify the largest size the image will ever display. For a full-width hero, that could be 1920 pixels wide on large screens, or more if you support high-density displays at wide viewports.

Your master image should be at least as large as that maximum rendered width. Upscaling a small image later almost always introduces blurriness or artifacts.

Modern image-generation models can follow detailed instructions, so describe the technical requirements in your prompt, not just the subject. Specify the aspect ratio, intended display size, visual style, and any areas that need to remain clear for HTML text. The exact controls available will depend on the tool you use, so check its official documentation before building a workflow around a particular feature.

A practical web-focused prompt might read: "hero image of a modern home office at sunrise, soft natural light, calm blue and warm wood tones, clear empty space on the left third for headline text, no text or logos in the image."

That last instruction matters. Avoid baking headlines or buttons into images. Text inside an image cannot be translated, resized for accessibility, or indexed reliably, and it often becomes unreadable at small sizes. Keep text in HTML and use the image for visuals only.

Once you have a master file, decide which formats to serve. For most photographic and illustrative AI images, a combination of AVIF, WebP, and JPEG covers every modern browser while keeping file sizes small.

AVIF typically offers the strongest compression for photographic content and is supported by all major modern browsers, including Safari 16 and later. WebP is slightly less efficient but encodes faster and has near-universal support. JPEG remains a reliable fallback for older browsers and email clients.

Use PNG only when you specifically need lossless quality, such as for sharp-edged graphics or screenshots. Both AVIF and WebP support transparency, so you rarely need PNG for images with transparent backgrounds anymore.

Creating a dozen versions of every image by hand is tedious and error-prone. Instead, script the process. The Sharp documentation explains how to resize images and export them in different formats.

Then create a script that exports several widths in each format:

const widths = [480, 768, 1080, 1440, 1920];

{ ext: 'avif', format: 'avif', options: { quality: 50 } },

{ ext: 'webp', format: 'webp', options: { quality: 75 } },

{ ext: 'jpg', format: 'jpeg', options: { quality: 80, mozjpeg: true } },

for (const { ext, format, options } of formats) {

.resize({ width, withoutEnlargement: true })

Save the file as an ES module, such as build-images.mjs, and run it with Node. The withoutEnlargement option prevents sharp from upscaling the master when a target width is larger than the original.

The quality values above are reasonable starting points, not universal rules. AVIF and WebP quality scales do not map directly to JPEG quality, so compare outputs visually at the sizes your users will actually see. Smooth gradients, which are common in AI-generated skies and backgrounds, are especially prone to banding at aggressive settings.

The MDN responsive images guide explains how srcset and sizes work. The srcset attribute lists available image files and their intrinsic widths. The sizes attribute tells the browser how wide the image will be displayed in the layout. With both pieces of information, the browser can choose the smallest file that still looks sharp on the visitor's screen, including high-density displays.

Here is an example for an image inside an article column that is 720 pixels wide on larger screens and nearly full width on smaller ones:

alt="A modern home office at sunrise with a wooden desk and soft natural light"

The most common mistake is omitting sizes or leaving it at 100vw for images that are not full width. When that happens, the browser assumes the image fills the entire viewport and downloads a much larger file than necessary. Always match sizes to your actual CSS layout.

To offer AVIF and WebP with a JPEG fallback, wrap your image in a picture element. The browser checks each source in order and uses the first format it supports. See the MDN documentation for the picture element for the full syntax.

srcset="dist/hero-768.avif 768w, dist/hero-1440.avif 1440w, dist/hero-1920.avif 1920w"

srcset="dist/hero-768.webp 768w, dist/hero-1440.webp 1440w, dist/hero-1920.webp 1920w"

srcset="dist/hero-768.jpg 768w, dist/hero-1440.jpg 1440w, dist/hero-1920.jpg 1920w"

alt="A modern home office at sunrise with a wooden desk and soft natural light"

The img element is still required. It holds the fallback file, the dimensions, the alt text, and the loading attributes, while the source elements simply provide alternative formats.

If you need a different crop on mobile, such as a square version of a wide hero, add media attributes to your source elements. This technique is called art direction, and it is a good reason to generate or crop a separate master image for small screens rather than relying on CSS to hide important parts of a wide composition.

Always include width and height attributes on your img element. Modern browsers use them to calculate the image's aspect ratio and reserve the correct space before the file downloads, which helps prevent Cumulative Layout Shift. In CSS, set the image to width: 100% and height: auto so it scales responsively while keeping its proportions.

Use loading="lazy" for images below the fold, but never on your hero or other LCP image. Lazy loading your most important image delays it unnecessarily. Instead, add fetchpriority="high" to the LCP image so the browser downloads it early.

Write alt text that describes the image's purpose in context. If an image is purely decorative, use an empty alt attribute so screen readers skip it. Generated images do not come with meaningful descriptions, so this step always requires human judgment.

Use descriptive file names, such as home-office-sunrise-1440.avif, instead of generic names like image-final-v3.png. Clear names make assets easier to manage and give search engines a small amount of extra context.

Be aware of metadata. Some AI image providers, including OpenAI, embed C2PA provenance data that identifies an image as AI-generated. sharp strips most metadata by default, which reduces file size but also removes that provenance information. If transparency matters to your project or your client, recent versions of sharp offer a keepMetadata() method, and you can also disclose AI-generated imagery in captions or credits.

In Chrome DevTools, open the Network panel, filter by images, and resize the viewport or switch to device emulation. Reload the page and confirm that smaller files load on smaller screens. You can also select the image in the Elements panel and check its currentSrc property in the console to see which file the browser actually chose.

Then run Lighthouse or PageSpeed Insights. Look for warnings about properly sized images, modern image formats, and LCP.

Not always. AVIF often produces smaller files for photographic content, but it encodes more slowly. Serving both with a JPEG fallback is a safe default.

Four to six widths usually cover most layouts. Choose them based on your breakpoints and the largest rendered size of each image.

Review the current terms of service for the model and the platform you use. Licensing terms can differ between providers and plans.

AI image generation removes much of the cost and time of creating custom visuals, but it does not remove the need for good web engineering. Generate a high-quality master at the right aspect ratio, export responsive variants in modern formats, write accurate srcset and sizes values, protect your LCP and layout stability, and test everything before you ship.

Once the pipeline is scripted, every new image takes seconds to optimize. That combination gives you the creative speed of AI and the performance your visitors expect.

#10603. Best Claude Tracking Tools in 2026: 6 Options Compared

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Most teams set up AI visibility tracking for ChatGPT, add Google, and stop there. Claude tends to come up later, usually when someone notices that half the engineers, analysts and founders they know use it every day. That instinct is sound. Claude's audience leans towards the people who research software and services before they buy.

The numbers back it up. Similarweb put Claude at 3.3% of AI chatbot web visits in February 2026 and 9.2% in May 2026, close to three times the share in three months, while ChatGPT's share kept falling. Those are web visits only. Usage in the Claude apps, in Claude Code and through the API does not show up in that figure, so 9.2% is a floor.

This guide compares six tools that track Claude. Peec AI comes first because it connects Claude answers to the pages behind them. The other five cover different budgets and needs.

A Claude tracking tool sends a fixed set of prompts to Claude on a schedule and records what comes back: whether your brand is named, where in the answer, how it is described, and which sources the answer relied on. Run daily, those records become trends you can compare against competitors.

It is not a rank tracker. Claude gives no list of ten blue links, so the useful numbers are mention rate, position inside the answer, sentiment and cited sources.

How the tool queries Claude. Some tools send your prompts to Anthropic's API. Others drive the Claude app. The two can give different answers, because the app has its own web search behaviour and the API, queried cold, often does not. Neither is wrong. Your buyers use the app, and the API is cheaper to run at scale. What matters is that you know which one you are looking at and that it stays the same over time.

Which plan includes Claude. Claude is a premium engine for several vendors. It can sit on the entry plan, on a higher tier or on Enterprise only, and a free tier often leaves it out.

What it costs per run. Credit-based tools can charge more for Claude than for other engines. Check the credit formula before you size a plan.

Source data. A mention rate says whether Claude names you. Source data says why it does not. Pick a tool that shows the pages Claude read.

Prompt volume. 50 to 150 prompts per brand is a realistic start. Fewer than 15 is mostly noise. Check how many prompts the cheaper tiers cover with Claude specifically: on credit-based tools Claude costs more per run, so the entry plan can cover far fewer Claude prompts than the headline number suggests.

Peec AI is a Berlin-based AI search analytics platform that tracks visibility, position, sentiment and share of voice across AI engines, then shows which sources drive those answers. Claude is part of the Enterprise plan and the agency Scale plan, tracked next to ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, Microsoft Copilot and both Google surfaces. That makes it the pick for teams that want Claude as one engine in a wider view rather than as a stand-alone report.

Best for: Teams that track Claude together with ChatGPT and Google and want to know which pages to work on, not only where they stand.

Scrunch AI tracks Claude on its Enterprise plan, alongside nine engines in total. The published Core plan at $250 a month covers four engines and leaves Claude out, so it suits teams that start with ChatGPT, Perplexity, Google and Copilot and add Claude when they move to a quote.

Best for: Teams that want a published entry price now and add Claude through an Enterprise contract later.

Rankscale puts Claude on every paid plan from $99 a month and covers the widest engine list at that price: Claude, Copilot, ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, both Google surfaces, DeepSeek and Mistral. It is credit-based, and the formula is published, which matters because Claude costs 2 credits per run, more than most engines. On Pro, 1,200 credits cover about 20 prompts run daily on Claude alone.

Best for: Small teams and agencies that want Claude and a long engine list for the least money.

AthenaHQ was built by two engineers who worked on Google Search and DeepMind. Claude is included from the Starter plan, among eleven engines. The free Essential tier does not include Claude, so it shows you the other engines first. Its optimisation agent drafts on-page and off-page recommendations, which suits teams that have the analysis but not the hands to act on it.

Best for: Teams short on people to write the follow-up work.

Profound is the shortest path for companies where an information security review decides the purchase. It lists SOC 2, SSO and SAML on Enterprise and raised a $96M Series C at a $1B valuation in February 2026. Claude is part of the Enterprise engine list, which runs to up to nine engines.

Best for: Enterprises that need a compliance posture on paper before they can buy.

Nightwatch is worth a look if you want Claude mentions next to the keyword rankings you already track and you are not paying for one of the large SEO suites. AI tracking is included in the plan price.

Best for: SEO teams that want one dashboard for classic rankings and Claude.

If Claude is one engine among several and you need to know what to fix, choose the tool with source analysis. If Claude is the only new engine and budget decides, Rankscale and Nightwatch cost the least. If you have a security review to pass, start with Profound or Peec AI's Enterprise plan. If you have no Claude coverage at all and cannot add a vendor, a few tools let you connect your own Anthropic API key, and Anthropic then bills you directly for the runs.

Claude is now a real share of the AI answers your buyers read, and its answers often differ from ChatGPT's. A single-engine number gives you false confidence in either direction. Peec AI is the strongest choice for teams that want Claude as part of a full view of sources, gaps and actions, with the caveat that Claude requires the Enterprise plan or, for agencies, the Scale plan. For the cheapest route to Claude coverage, Rankscale and Nightwatch are the practical options, though Rankscale's entry plan covers only about 20 daily Claude prompts, against 50 AI prompts on Nightwatch's entry plan. Whichever you choose, ask how the tool queries Claude and keep that method fixed. A tool measures. What moves the number is being on the pages Claude reads, and the best Claude tracking tools show you which ones those are.

No. If you can add one engine after ChatGPT, add Gemini, because its share is about three times larger. Add Claude third, and earlier if your buyers are technical.

Does Claude cite the same sources as ChatGPT?

Often not, and that is the practical reason to track it. Being named in one engine tells you little about the other.

With some tools, yes. Gauge lets you connect your own key on any plan, and Anthropic bills you directly for the runs. It is a cheap way to add Claude if your main tool does not include it.

How do I turn Claude tracking results into something I can act on?

Look for source data, not only a mention rate. A mention rate says whether Claude names you, while source data shows which pages Claude relied on and where competitors are cited and you are not. Peec AI classifies every cited page, reports the gaps and ranks recommended actions from them, and AthenaHQ goes a step further by drafting follow-up content. Tools that stop at mention counts tell you where you stand but not what to change.
